# [21/159] Sectors/Copper-Clad Laminate & PCB Materials.md
**sector · status: active · sector: Copper-Clad Laminate & PCB Materials · date: 2026-06-10**

High-speed copper-clad laminate (CCL) and prepreg: the glass-fabric-reinforced, copper-foil-clad dielectric that forms the printed circuit boards beneath AI accelerators (GPU baseboards, HGX/UBB carriers, 1.6T switch trays, NIC cards). The "M-grade" loss spec (M4→M9, now M10) governs signal integrity at 112G/224G/448G SerDes. CCL sits one layer below [[Sectors/ABF Substrates & Advanced Packaging Supply Chain]] (the IC-package carrier) and is gated upstream by a low-Dk glass-cloth near-monopoly ([[Theses/3110 - Nitto Boseki]]). A ~US$17B CCL market has **bifurcated into two industries**: a ~$13B commodity FR-4 base (China-led, cyclical, ~6% CAGR) and a ~$4B high-speed/AI premium (Taiwan/Japan-led, de-commoditizing, ~10% CAGR with the AI-server sub-slice compounding ~20%+); and the market still prices the second through the lens of the first. Specialty AI/radar grades already carry 30–50% price premiums over commodity FR-4, and that spread is widening, not mean-reverting.

AI did not just grow CCL demand, it **moved the bottleneck up the stack**. The binding constraint is no longer the laminator's press but the three scarce inputs the laminator is allocated (low-Dk glass cloth, HVLP copper foil, low-loss PPE resin), each a Japan/Taiwan oligopoly, each sold out, each compounding the leaders' moat ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #1, #8). This note maps all four layers (glass/foil/resin → CCL → PCB fab → ODM) because the AI-PCB value pool is being fought over at every one.

## Active Theses
- [[Theses/2383 - Elite Material]] (2383.TW, draft → MEDIUM): global #1 high-speed CCL (~28% share); the toll road under hyperscaler ASIC + 1.6T switch boards (~100% Meta MTIA, ~80% AWS Trainium, ~50% Google TPU). Pending promotion via `/status`.
- [[Theses/3110 - Nitto Boseki]] (3110.JP, draft → MEDIUM): the upstream glass-cloth near-monopoly (~90% T-glass, ~60–70% NER-glass) that gates this sector and the ABF-substrate stack. Pending promotion via `/status`.

*Adjacent investable names not yet in book (watchlist: see §Investor heuristics → Cross-vault attractiveness): Panasonic (6752.JP, Megtron benchmark), TUC (6274.TW), ITEQ (6213.TW), Shengyi (600183.SS, the China high-end wildcard), Kingboard (0148.HK, vertical-integration play), Mitsui Mining & Smelting (5706.JP, #1 HVLP foil), Zhen Ding (4958.TW)/Victory Giant (HK-listed, NVIDIA AI-PCB share-gainer) at the PCB-fab layer.*

## Key industry questions
- **Does the high-end premium survive the synchronized 2027 capacity vintage?** EMC, TUC, ITEQ, Panasonic, Shengyi and Nan Ya are all adding high-end lines, bunched into one ~2027 start-up wave by the ~2-year equipment lead (vacuum-press/treater orders are now booked through 2028). High-end specialty premia have historically compressed once capacity catches demand; the central tension of the sector ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #6, #17).
- **Does the China volume cohort (Kingboard, Shengyi) climb the grade curve to contest the Taiwan/Japan quality leaders?** Shengyi is already NVIDIA-qualified (Synamic9GN) and reportedly progressing toward M10; state-backed, captive China demand. Qualified M8 at a Western hyperscaler by 2027 would cap the incumbents' China TAM and anchor high-end price.
- **Does the upstream input bottleneck stay a moat-widener or flip to margin compression?** Three scarce inputs (Nittobo glass, HVLP copper foil, PPE resin) entrench the largest CCL buyers today; if mid-2027 capacity across all three lands while AI demand cools, pass-through cover and the allocation barrier disappear together.
- **Does architecture substitution erode CCL content?** Glass-core substrates (the layer above), CPO/optics, and panel-level packaging could each reduce PCB layer count and per-board CCL content at the very leading edge; long-dated (2027–2030+) but real ([[Macro & Technology/Organic ABF to Glass-Core Substrate Transition]]).
- **Where in the AI-PCB chain does the value actually pool: material, fabricator, or foil?** CCL is ~30–40% of a high-layer-count AI board's bill of materials, but the PCB fabricator (Zhen Ding, Victory Giant, Unimicron) captures the assembly margin and the foil/glass/resin makers capture the scarce-input rent. The investable question is which layer holds pricing power through the cycle.
- **What is the ROIC of the supply response to 2030?** The variable that decides whether the capacity build is disciplined (high-ROIC, price-supportive) or destructive (ROIC-insensitive state-backed supply compressing ASP).

## Competitive dynamics

The sector is **two competitive arenas that share a name**:

**Arena 1: commodity FR-4 (volume game, China-led).** Won on scale, cost and vertical integration. Cyclical, priced on copper/resin spreads, ~6% CAGR. ~$13B of the ~$17B total.

**Arena 2: high-speed / AI CCL (spec-in game, Taiwan/Japan-led).** Won on resin chemistry, qualification, first-mover and scarce-input allocation. De-commoditizing, margin-expanding, ~10% CAGR with the AI-server sub-slice ~20%+. ~$4B and the entire profit-growth engine.

### Market sizing — the bifurcation in numbers

| Segment | 2025 size | Trajectory | Economics |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Total CCL** | ~US$16.8B | → ~$24B by 2031 (~6% CAGR) | Blended; commodity-weighted |
| Commodity FR-4 (bulk) | ~$12–13B | ~5–6% CAGR | Cyclical, copper/resin spread, low-margin |
| **High-freq/high-speed CCL** | ~$4.1B | → ~$10.9B by 2035 (~10% CAGR) | Spec-in; 30–50% price premium |
| - AI-server CCL sub-slice | ~$1.5–2B (est.) | → ~$3.5B by 2031 (~20% CAGR) | Fastest slice; high-30s% incremental GM |
| Downstream PCB (for scale) | ~$96B | → ~$127B by 2031 | 40+ layer AI boards ~4× the ASP of 8-layer boards |

The market still applies a blended ~6%-CAGR commodity lens to a high-speed franchise compounding 2–3× faster at expanding margin; the durability of the margin, not the growth, is what is mispriced.

### Competitive matrix

| Player | Listing | Arena strength | AI / high-speed position |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Kingboard Laminates** | 0148.HK | #1 by *total volume*; fully integrated (copper foil, glass yarn/fabric, resin) | Commodity-weighted; climbing high-speed slowly; investing into e-grade glass yarn/fabric (Shixing, ~$260M) |
| **Shengyi / SYTECH** | 600183.SS | #2 by volume since 2013; state-backed; total CCL capacity → >100M m²/yr | NVIDIA-qualified (Synamic9GN), reportedly progressing to M10; the China high-end wildcard for 2027 |
| **Nan Ya Plastics** | 1303.TW | Top-3 volume (Formosa scale); also makes copper foil + glass cloth | Secondary high-speed; licensed ~20% of Nittobo specialty glass by 2027 |
| **Elite Material (EMC)** | 2383.TW | **#1 high-speed (~28% global high-speed share)**; halogen-free leader since 2013 | ~100% Meta MTIA, ~80% AWS Trainium, ~50% Google TPU, 50–60% 800G/1.6T switch; M7+ >60% of rev |
| **Panasonic (Megtron)** | 6752.JP | The **quality benchmark** (Megtron 8 Df ~0.0015), capacity-constrained, higher-cost | Premium incumbent; doubling Megtron capacity in Thailand (~$110M/5yr) |
| **TUC (Taiwan Union)** | 6274.TW | #2 Taiwan high-speed; ThunderClad 200G/400G/800G (2021) | Strong on NVIDIA GPU boards; ~1/3 EMC's scale, growing ~28% |
| **ITEQ** | 6213.TW | #3 Taiwan; high-speed + RF | TUC+ITEQ together ~18% of global high-frequency/high-speed |
| **AGC Multi Materials / Doosan / Isola / Rogers / Resonac** | various | Legacy high-performance (PTFE, RF) | Tier-2 AI exposure; strongest at the RF/switch PTFE end |

### The real leading-edge replicator set is only ~3
At M8/M8.5/M9 qualified for Western-hyperscaler ASIC + Rubin boards, only **EMC, Panasonic and TUC** genuinely compete today, far narrower than the eight-name matrix implies. Panasonic is the quality peer but capacity-constrained and higher-cost; TUC is a credible half-step behind at ~1/3 EMC's scale. **Shengyi is the most likely fourth entrant by 2027**: the state-backed, captive-China structural threat. This is the qualification-gate-monopoly pattern hidden behind tonnage share data ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #2): screens that rank CCL by volume surface Kingboard/Shengyi and miss that the AI-relevant franchise is a 3-player high-speed oligopoly gated by a near-monopoly input.

### The M9 node contest: quartz breaks Nittobo's glass-chemistry gate, and the impact splits sharply across the two names
M9 (NVIDIA's internal spec: **Df ≤0.0007, Dk <3.0 at 10 GHz**; mass production **2H 2026**; mandated for the **78-layer Rubin Ultra orthogonal backplane** and 1.6T switch/backplane trays) is the first grade where the reinforcement changes *material class*, not just formulation. M8/M8.5 ran on evolved low-Dk **glass fiber** (Nittobo NE/NER, "Low Dk1/Dk2"); M9 ("Low Dk3") moves to **quartz cloth, ~99.9%-silica "Q-glass"**, a different material that bypasses the borosilicate glass-chemistry gate Nittobo's ~90% share is built on. This is [[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #8 (architecture transition remaps the bottleneck) firing one layer below CCL.

| Attribute | Nittobo **NEZ** (evolved glass fiber) | Asahi-cohort **Q-glass** (quartz) |
|---|---|---|
| Composition | low-Dk borosilicate | **~99.9% silica (quartz)** |
| Dk @ 10 GHz | ~**4.0** | ~**3.7** |
| Df @ 10 GHz | ~0.001-class | ~**0.0005** (intrinsic quartz → ~0.0002) |
| CTE | low | ~**0.5 ppm/°C** (near-zero) |
| Cost | ~**$25–30/m** | ~**$50/m (1.7–2×)** |
| Processing | mature | **harder: drill-bit wear + residual fiber protrusion in vias → copper-plating yield risk** |

M9 CCL runs **~15–20× FR-4** (M8 ~10–15×, M7 ~6–9×); M9/Q-glass lead times are **20+ weeks, allocation-only**.

**The upstream layer fragments rather than handing off.** Nittobo's ~90% dominance is in T-glass (substrate, Low CTE) and NER-glass (Low Dk2, M8-class); at the quartz tier it is not the franchise. Per TrendForce, "Low Dk3 (Q-glass)" is a **cohort: Asahi Kasei, Shin-Etsu (SQX), Glotech, Feilihua, Taishan Fiberglass, Hong Ho, "collectively capturing the majority share in the early stages" of M9.** Nittobo's M9 answer, NEZ, is an evolved glass fiber (Dk ~4.0), a structural half-step behind quartz on both loss and CTE, backstopped by a next-gen T-glass slated for 2028. The "Asahi quartz takes the early M9 majority" read is therefore directionally right but more precisely a **quartz-cohort** story, and the next node is **less monopolistic upstream**, not a monopoly changing hands.

**Nittobo (3110): existential to the leading edge, bounded elsewhere.** Quartz taking the early M9 majority fires the thesis's own **→ LOW trigger** and is the single falsifying datapoint its stress test flagged ([[Research/2026-06-26 - 3110 - Stress Test]]): the ~90% share is **node-bound**, and the qualification-gate moat ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #2) does not reach a chemistry Nittobo does not lead. Damage bounds: M9 is the *smallest, newest* slice (switch-tray/backplane, not the larger M8/M8.5 compute-tray volume that stays on glass fiber); quartz's ~2× cost and harder processing keep glass fiber in cost-sensitive layers; and the T-glass substrate franchise is a *separate* contest where quartz's 0.5 ppm/°C CTE is a longer-dated second front, not an immediate one. Net: quartz caps Nittobo at the trailing-grade ceiling at the exact node that sets forward value, without erasing the M8-class + substrate base: a monopoly multiple on an oligopoly franchise, not a franchise gone.

**EMC (2383): moat-modifier, sign ambiguous-to-negative, and more contested than "it just changes our supplier."** Three effects, not one. (1) **Allocation-moat erosion**: EMC's Insight-#3 edge (scarce Nittobo glass allocated to the largest qualified buyer, starving sub-scale rivals) weakens, because the quartz cohort adds new qualified suppliers who can feed EMC's competitors; the chokepoint that entrenched EMC dissolves into a 6-supplier quartz field. (2) **Supply-diversification upside**: EMC grows less hostage to Nittobo's 40–55% price hikes. (3) **The negative the vault missed: a material-class change resets CCL qualification, and EMC is not clearly ahead at M9.** Halogen-free *resin* IP does not confer *quartz-lamination* mastery (a different drilling/plating yield problem). Per Digitimes (Nov 2025), **Doosan (DS-7409 M9Q) emerged as the early M9-quartz volume leader and is "poised to secure exclusive Nvidia Rubin CCL supply as EMC failed a GB300 test,"** with EMC pushing **EM-896K3** to close the gap and Shengyi developing equivalents. This updates the replicator set above for the M9 sub-node: the "EMC/Panasonic/TUC-only" leading edge gains **Doosan as the early M9 front-runner**, and EMC's incumbency is not a given. Hold as a hypothesis to test: single channel-check source, and Goldman's Sept-2025 check had EMC "benefiting most" on Rubin; the contradiction is itself the signal that the M9 socket is live, not settled.

**Cross-thesis synthesis (value-layer-monopoly lens).** The M9/quartz transition is adverse for *both halves of the toll road at once*: upstream the rent **disperses** (fragmented quartz cohort vs Nittobo's clean glass monopoly); downstream the CCL leadership **reshuffles** (Doosan up, EMC contested). The node the bull case prices as more content-per-board (true) is also **less monopolistic at the layer that mattered**: the toll booth relocates from Nittobo's loom to a contested quartz field, and neither incumbent automatically collects it. Falsifiable signals: M9 design-win splits (Nittobo NEZ vs quartz cohort) as 224G qualifies through 2026–27; EMC EM-896K3 qualification on Rubin switch trays; confirmation or reversal of Doosan's Rubin exclusivity; and whether quartz's cost/yield penalty caps it at the switch-tray niche while M8/M8.5 glass-fiber volume (and Nittobo's allocation moat) holds through 2027.

### Anchor-customer concentration is a survival test, not a footnote
EMC's ~100% share on Meta MTIA, ~80% on AWS Trainium and 50–60% on 1.6T switch fabric is the qualification-gate moat and the binary risk ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #10): a 6–18-month qualification locks the socket for the product's life, but the loss of a single flagship socket (MTIA, Trainium) to Shengyi at M8 would be the confirmation the moat broke at the leading edge, the CLOSE trigger in the EMC thesis. Concentration cuts both ways: it locks sockets in but hands large customers leverage on price in a soft demand window.

### Capacity roadmap — the synchronized 2027 vintage

| Player | Expansion | Timing | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EMC** | → 9.45M sheets/month (Taiwan + China + Malaysia); Guanyin NT$12.4B + Taoyuan high-end build | Peak ramp 2027 | The volume + breadth leader |
| **Panasonic** | Doubling Megtron capacity, Thailand (~$110M/5yr) | 2026–2027 | Quality benchmark, deliberately paced |
| **Shengyi** | Multi-site; total CCL → >100M m²/yr; high-frequency ramping since 1H 2025 | 2026–2027 | State-backed; the ROIC-insensitive marginal supplier |
| **TUC / ITEQ / Nan Ya** | All adding high-end lines | 2026–2027 | Bunched by ~2yr equipment lead |
| **Equipment (vacuum press + treater)** | Orders booked through 2028; ~2-year delivery | — | The pacing constraint and a 2027 oversupply trigger |

Everyone is building high-end lines at once, and the ~2-year equipment lead synchronizes the start-ups into a single **2027 vintage**, the first real read on whether the high-end specialty premium survives capacity catching demand. This is the classic semi capital-cycle setup: a delayed, equipment-gated supply response calibrated to inflated shortage prices, where the down-leg risk is sharpest precisely when the build lands into the first plausible AI digestion ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #3, #17).

### Pricing-power trajectory and the price-hike decomposition
High-end is de-commoditizing, margin expanding into the build (EMC GM 30.1%, +3.1pp YoY) while 20–40% price hikes stick, versus commodity FR-4 reverting to spread economics in any downturn. The hikes are mostly genuine pricing power, not glass pass-through: glass is only ~15–20% of high-end material cost, so a +20–30% Nittobo hike is ~3–6% of COGS, leaving the bulk of a 20–40% price increase as margin capture. Pure pass-through never expands margin; margin expansion through rising input costs is the tell. The honest caveat: part of the capture is cyclical shortage-rent (allocation power while inputs are sold out) versus structural spec-in pricing, and that split is the entire durability question into the 2027 vintage.

### The ROIC bifurcation (the sector's central tension)
Incremental high-end capacity earns >25–30% ROIC today in a sold-out market, which is why everyone builds. To 2030 it splits: the disciplined leaders (EMC, Panasonic) defend a premium-ROIC core, but the *industry marginal* ROIC is set by the least-disciplined entrant. **State-backed Chinese capacity (Shengyi) is structurally ROIC-insensitive**: it adds high-end lines for sovereignty reasons even below cost of capital, and that is the mechanism that compresses high-end ASP and turns a high-ROIC specialty into a mid-ROIC cyclical if AI demand decelerates as the 2027 vintage lands. The gap between EMC's *defended* ROIC and the *compressing industry marginal* ROIC is the MEDIUM-versus-HIGH conviction question for the whole sector.

### Process-moat depth, calibrated
CCL's process moat is real but ~1–2 orders of magnitude shallower than a leading-edge foundry or memory maker (capex ~$0.5B/line vs $15–30B/fab; ~7–10 process steps vs hundreds-to-1,500; 5–6 rivals vs 2–3). Durability rests on a re-compounding stack (materials-IP + per-node qualification + first-mover + scarce-input allocation), not irreproducible process physics. The calibration the whole sector hangs on: **wider than "commodity laminate," narrower than "TSMC-grade monopoly."** It classifies as a semi-cyclical compounder, not a structural compounder ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #13): the qualification gate keeps the down-cycle margin shallower than the FR-4 template, but the 5–6-player oligopoly and ROIC-insensitive marginal supplier prevent the monopoly economics the bulls imply.

### The value chain and where margin pools sit

| Layer | Key players | Pricing power | AI rent capture |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Raw batch** (silica sand, boron, electrolytic copper, petrochemical resin precursors) | Commodity miners/chemicals | None | None |
| **Low-Dk glass cloth** | **Nittobo (~90% T-glass)**, Asahi Kasei (quartz), Taiwan Glass, Nan Ya | **Highest**: sole-source at top grade | Deepest monopoly; smallest market (~$4B) |
| **HVLP copper foil** | Mitsui Mining & Smelting (#1), JX Nippon, Furukawa, ILJIN, Circuit Foil, Chang Chun, Nan Ya | High: sold out, 3-yr shortfall | Scarce-input rent; vertical integrators (Chang Chun, Nan Ya) capture both layers |
| **Low-loss resin** (PPE/PPO oligomer, BMI, hydrocarbon, PTFE) | SABIC (NORYL SA9000), Asahi Kasei, Mitsubishi Chemical | High at PPE oligomer | The chemistry IP layer; tight, expanding capacity |
| **CCL / prepreg** | **EMC, Panasonic, TUC, ITEQ, Shengyi, Kingboard, Nan Ya** | High at high-speed; low at FR-4 | The spec-in toll road; ~30–40% of board BOM |
| **PCB fabrication** | **Zhen Ding (#1), Unimicron, Victory Giant, Tripod, Compeq, WUS, Shennan, AT&S, Meiko** | Medium: assembly margin, capex-heavy | Captures board-build margin; 40+ layer ASP ~4× standard |
| **ODM / system** | Foxconn/Hon Hai, Quanta, Wistron/Wiwynn | Low: pass-through assemblers | Volume, thin margin |
| **End customer** | NVIDIA + hyperscalers (Meta, AWS, Google, Microsoft) | Sets the spec; pays the bill | Funds the whole chain via AI capex |

The structural read: **pricing power concentrates at the two most-upstream scarce-input layers (glass, foil) and at the spec-in CCL layer, and is inversely proportional to position size in the market.** The deepest monopoly (Nittobo, ~$4.2B mcap) is the smallest and least-owned; the most-owned names sit downstream where the moat is shallower. Own the stack, not a single layer ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #1, #2).

## Macro shifts

- **AI board-complexity escalation**: content-per-board compounds on three axes (board count × layer count × material grade); CCL revenue per AI rack grows even if accelerator units decelerate. The cleanest content-escalation tailwind in the AI hardware stack, and largely orthogonal to the unit-growth S-curve.
- **The SerDes data-rate ladder** (112G/~28GHz → 224G/~56GHz → 448G) drives the grade ladder (M7→M9→M10→beyond) on a roughly per-generation cadence; material that was leading-edge two years ago is mid-tier today. This is the architecture transition that keeps re-locating the bottleneck and re-compounding the leaders' qualification lead ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #8).
- **Custom-silicon ASIC migration**: the high-speed CCL leaders are the toll road paid whether NVIDIA or hyperscaler ASICs win (EMC dominant on Meta MTIA / AWS Trainium / Google TPU). A rare hedge against the most-debated question in the AI trade. Cross-reference [[Sectors/Custom Silicon & Networking Semiconductors]], [[Sectors/Compute & AI Compute Accelerators]].
- **Triple upstream input bottleneck**: (1) Nittobo low-Dk glass cloth (~90% T-glass, sold out through end-2026, capacity mid-2027 earliest); (2) HVLP copper foil (Goldman's "new normal" 3-year shortfall); (3) PPE/PPO resin (tight, expanding). Each is a Japan/Taiwan oligopoly, each is the leaders' allocation moat and a cost risk if pass-through stalls.
- **Architecture-substitution risk**: glass-core substrates ([[Macro & Technology/Organic ABF to Glass-Core Substrate Transition]]), CPO/optical interconnect ([[Sectors/Optical Networking & Photonics]]) and panel-level packaging could each plateau PCB layer count and per-board CCL content at the leading edge (2027–2030+). Glass-core hits the *substrate* layer above CCL first; CPO moves some 224G electrical routing onto optics inside the rack, the long-dated bear vector on content escalation.
- **China localization / geopolitical bifurcation**: state-backed Chinese CCL is the ROIC-insensitive supply that anchors high-end price down; a captive China AI-server market (Chinese AI chips ~41% of local AI-server shipments in 2025) walls off TAM into a parallel market with independent supply/demand ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #16). Shengyi + Victory Giant + Kingboard are building a vertically-integrated domestic stack from glass to board.
- **The synchronized 2027 capacity vintage**: equipment lead times (~2 years on vacuum presses + treater lines, booked through 2028) bunch the industry's adds into one wave; 2027 is the first read on high-end oversupply / ASP direction. The single most important dated catalyst for the sector.
- **Where on the S-curve**: high-speed AI CCL sits mid-chasm: the S-curve is secured (every AI board needs it) but timing and margin durability are uncertain, the highest-edge zone for long-term capital, and the zone where the cycle-vs-structural decomposition matters most ([[Mental Models/Generalist - Overview]] #4, [[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #18). The error to avoid is reading the 2024–2026 margin expansion as either pure cycle (it has a structural spec-in component) or pure structure (it has a real shortage-rent component).

## Investor heuristics

### Current consensus and what is priced in
Consensus still half-prices CCL as a cyclical commodity laminate (the FR-4 / copper-spread frame) despite the high-end de-commoditizing. The growth is seen; the durability of the high-end margin through the 2027 vintage is not: that is the mispricing. The high-speed leaders are crowded longs (EMC sell-side 14 buy / 0 sell), so the marginal-bull risk sits downstream at the most-owned names; the upstream monopoly (Nittobo) is more balanced (Goldman Neutral) and far less owned.

### The screen traps
- **Volume leadership ≠ quality leadership.** Tonnage screens surface Kingboard/Shengyi; the AI-relevant franchise is the Taiwan/Japan high-speed cluster (EMC, Panasonic, TUC) and the upstream glass monopoly (Nittobo).
- **Trailing P/E is a mirage at the upstream names.** Nittobo's trailing ~16x is inflated by one-off asset-sale gains; the clean number is ~35x forward: diligence the recurring margin, not the headline.
- **"AI server units" undercounts CCL.** Content-per-board escalation (layer × grade × board count) grows CCL revenue independent of unit growth; unit-pegged models understate the franchise.

### Own the toll-road stack, not a single layer
The most-upstream chokepoint (Nittobo glass, ~90% share, ~$4.2B mcap) is far smaller than its downstream customer (EMC, ~28% high-speed share, ~$57B); the deepest monopoly is the least-owned. Pricing power is inversely proportional to market-cap position in this chain. The two are an upstream/downstream pair on one toll road; the foil layer (Mitsui et al.) is a third, even-less-owned scarce-input rent.

### Cross-vault attractiveness assessment
Ranking the investable layers by moat depth × under-ownership × AI-rent capture:

| Name | Layer | Moat | Setup | Vault status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Nittobo (3110.JP)** | Glass cloth | Deepest (~90% T-glass, sole-source) | Most under-owned ($4.2B); node risk (Asahi quartz at M9) | **Thesis, draft MEDIUM** |
| **EMC (2383.TW)** | High-speed CCL | Strong (#1, ~28%, anchor sockets) | Crowded (+542% LTM, ~47x fwd); 2027-vintage risk | **Thesis, draft MEDIUM** |
| Panasonic (6752.JP) | CCL (Megtron) | Quality benchmark | Buried in a conglomerate; capacity-constrained | Watchlist |
| Mitsui M&S (5706.JP) | HVLP foil | High (#1 foil, sold out) | Under-discussed; 3-yr shortfall | Watchlist: `/thesis` candidate |
| Shengyi (600183.SS) | CCL (China) | Rising; state-backed | The bear's instrument (ROIC-insensitive marginal) | Monitor (competitive swing) |
| Victory Giant / Zhen Ding | PCB fab | Medium (assembly margin) | Victory Giant +70% rev '26; concentration risk | Watchlist: value-pool claim |

The cleanest structural play is the *least-owned upstream monopoly* (Nittobo); the highest-quality downstream franchise (EMC) is correctly identified but richly priced into a synchronized build. The HVLP foil layer (Mitsui) is the under-covered third scarce input worth a `/thesis`.

### Non-consensus reads
1. **Margin durability through the 2027 vintage** is the debate, not growth, and it decomposes into shortage-rent (fades) + structural spec-in (persists); the split is the call.
2. **The upstream input bottleneck is a moat-widener, not just a cost headwind**: scarce glass/foil/resin is allocated to the largest qualified buyers, starving sub-scale rivals of inputs they cannot qualify around inside two years.
3. **The ROIC bifurcation** (a defended-leader premium ROIC vs an ROIC-insensitive state-backed marginal supplier) is what converts (or doesn't) a high-ROIC specialty into a mid-ROIC cyclical.
4. **The moat is materials-IP + qualification + first-mover + scarce-input allocation**, wider than commodity, narrower than monopoly, which is why the high-speed names warrant MEDIUM, not HIGH, conviction into a synchronized capacity build, and classify as semi-cyclical compounders rather than structural compounders ([[Mental Models/Industry - Semiconductors]] #13).
5. **Value pools at the scarce-input layers** (glass > foil > resin) more durably than at CCL or PCB fab, and those layers are the least-owned in the vault.

# [22/159] Sectors/Custom Silicon & Networking Semiconductors.md
**sector · status: active · date: 2026-04-22**

## Active Theses
- [[Theses/AVGO - Broadcom]]: Broadcom (custom ASIC + networking silicon dual franchise, 5 XPU customers, 80–90% merchant switching share, $100B+ 2027 AI revenue target, VMware software annuity; conviction: high)
- [[Theses/MRVL - Marvell Technology]]: Marvell (second-source ASIC design partner, 80%+ optical DSP share at 800G, Celestial AI Photonic Fabric memory-disaggregation bet, $2B Nvidia NVLink Fusion deal March 2026; conviction: medium)

## Key industry questions
- Is the AI data-center fabric economically a chokepoint (Broadcom's 80–90% merchant switching share + ~60–70% custom ASIC share as a structural "picks-and-shovels" monopoly) or a contestable commodity (Marvell/Alchip/MediaTek multi-sourcing, Nvidia Spectrum-X + NVLink Fusion, UALink/SUE/ESUN scale-up fragmentation) over the 2026–2030 horizon?
- Will custom XPUs (Google Ironwood, Meta MTIA, AWS Trainium, OpenAI XPU, Anthropic rack-scale TPU) cannibalize Nvidia GPU share above or below the ~30% ceiling implied by current hyperscaler capex mix, and how much of the resulting ASIC revenue accrues to silicon design partners (Broadcom/Marvell/Alchip) vs is internalized by the hyperscalers themselves?
- Does Ethernet displace InfiniBand in back-end AI training by 2027 (Dell'Oro base case), and if so, does Broadcom's Tomahawk/Jericho franchise capture the architectural rent or does Nvidia's Spectrum-X + NVLink Fusion recapture it via semi-custom bundling?
- Will NVLink Fusion (Nvidia + Marvell + MediaTek + Alchip + Astera Labs, March 2026 $2B Nvidia–Marvell deal) or UALink 1.0 (AMD + Intel + Google + Meta + Microsoft + HPE) win the 2027–2028 hyperscaler scale-up rack standard, and does Broadcom's Tomahawk Ultra / SUE third-path benefit either way as the only merchant-silicon scale-up substrate already shipping in volume in 2026?
- Does Linear Pluggable Optics (LPO) compress merchant optical DSP gross margin from ~65% to ~55% by FY28 (Marvell shipping the industry-first 1.6T LPO chipset is a deliberate margin-destructive hedge against its own DSP monopoly), and is the resulting blended optical economics positive or negative for the silicon design partners as 1.6T port-count growth offsets the ASP loss?
- Is the second-source structural slot a permanent procurement feature (every hyperscaler RFP is bid by Broadcom + Marvell to avoid single-vendor lock-in) or a transitional state that collapses by 2028 as one design partner achieves an unbridgeable IP / packaging / SerDes lead, and what does "second-seat ceiling" pricing mean for Marvell's ability to ever close the AVGO ~65% to MRVL ~60% gross-margin gap?

## Competitive dynamics

The sector has an unusually asymmetric structure: one incumbent (Broadcom) holds simultaneous dominance in two adjacent franchises (merchant switching silicon + custom ASIC design services), surrounded by specialists attacking each franchise separately. The cross-franchise leverage (shared SerDes IP, shared packaging, shared TSMC allocation, shared hyperscaler relationships) is the durable edge that single-franchise challengers cannot replicate, and it is strengthening rather than weakening as workloads scale.

| Company | Custom ASIC / XPU share | Merchant switching silicon | Scale-up fabric posture | Primary hyperscaler customers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Broadcom (AVGO)** | ~60–70% (Counterpoint: ~60% by 2027); XPU revenue 65% of AI segment | 80–90% merchant share; Tomahawk 6 at 102.4 Tbps shipping March 2026, 2+ quarters ahead of Nvidia | Scale-Up Ethernet (SUE) submitted to OCP; Tomahawk Ultra 51.2 Tbps at 250ns latency | Google (since 2013, all 7 TPU gens), Meta (4 MTIA gens, 1GW commitment), OpenAI (10GW deal), Anthropic (3.5GW TPU-Broadcom racks), ByteDance |
| **Marvell (MRVL)** | ~13–25% (Counterpoint: ~25% by 2027); FY2026E ASIC revenue $9–11B | Teralynx trails 1–2 gens (12.8 Tbps shipping vs AVGO 102.4 Tbps); Teralynx unit forecast only 1.8M by 2028 | NVLink Fusion partner (March 2026 $2B Nvidia deal); Celestial AI $3.25B acquisition for Photonic Fabric | AWS (Trainium 2: lost Trainium 3 socket to Alchip; reportedly regaining partial T3 work on chiplet), Microsoft (Maia DPU), Meta (new DPU), Google (inference chip talks April 2026) |
| **Alchip (3661.TW)** | ~5–10%, growing fastest | None | NVLink Fusion partner | AWS Trainium 3 (won from Marvell: back-end physical design + package design); Google TPU back-end support |
| **MediaTek (2454.TW)** | Emerging (~2–5%); Google's third XPU partner | None | NVLink Fusion partner | Google (inference-optimized TPU alongside Broadcom + Marvell) |
| **Nvidia (NVDA)** | Internal only (Blackwell/Rubin/Feynman GPUs); does not design ASICs for others | Spectrum-X Ethernet: Q1 2025 revenue +760% YoY to $1.46B = ~21% data-center switch revenue share; Spectrum-X1600 (102.4 Tbps) slips to H2 2026 (6+ months behind Tomahawk 6) | NVLink + NVLink Fusion (opens scale-up socket to ecosystem while retaining royalty + toll); $2B invested in Marvell March 2026 | All, but as chip vendor, not silicon design partner |
| **Arista (ANET)** | None | Systems vendor on Broadcom silicon; #1 data-center switch revenue share Q1 2025 (~21.5%) | Systems partner for SUE deployments | Meta, Microsoft primary; broad enterprise/hyperscaler base |
| **Cisco (CSCO)** | None | Silicon One (own silicon, launched 2019); data-center segment share collapsed from 78% (2012) to ~18% (Q1 2025); 27–28% YoY segment decline FY2024 | NVIDIA partnership on Spectrum-X; own Silicon One may be deprioritized | Enterprise + campus; diminishing hyperscaler presence |
| **AMD** | Pensando DPU (2022 acquisition $1.9B); Pollara 400 first UEC-ready 400G AI NIC | No merchant switching silicon | UALink founding member; "UALoE" (UALink-over-Ethernet) tunneling as interim; ESUN contributor | Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud, IBM Cloud (DPU deployments) |
| **Astera Labs (ALAB)** | None: connectivity pure-play | Scorpio Smart Fabric Switch launched volume early 2026 ($20B switching-segment entry) | PCIe/CXL retimers + smart cable modules + NVLink Fusion scale-up connectivity | All six US hyperscalers; FY2025 revenue ~$830M (from $116M in 2023) |
| **Credo (CRDO)** | None | DSPs for active electrical cables (AEC); SerDes IP | None: focuses on short-reach copper interconnect | Microsoft, Meta, Amazon (AEC deployments) |
| **Intel (INTC)** | ASIC design services pivot (post-Barefoot/Tofino exit) | Exited merchant switching silicon | Not a participant | None material |
| **Huawei (Ascend)** | Vertically integrated (own architecture + own HBM + own CANN software), not a merchant design services competitor | Proprietary Atlas SuperPoD fabric; not merchant | Proprietary | China-domestic (ByteDance $5.6B 950PR order, 750K units in 2026) |

**Marvell's structural position is the procurement complement to Broadcom, not a technical peer.** Hyperscalers do not accept single-vendor lock-in on multi-billion-dollar custom-silicon programs, so every RFP that goes to Broadcom is also shopped to a credible alternate. Alchip is Taiwan-only ownership (geopolitical concentration), MediaTek is mobile-first with limited HPC SerDes IP, GUC is sub-scale; by elimination, Marvell occupies the second-source structural slot in 2026. Two consequences flow from this: (i) the floor revenue is durable even if Marvell never closes the Broadcom technical gap because the procurement slot exists regardless of product gap; (ii) the same procurement logic that hands Marvell sockets caps its pricing power: every "second seat" is structurally lower-margin than the incumbent's, which is the empirical reading of MRVL ~60% non-GAAP gross margin vs AVGO ~65% (vs Alchip ~30% as the pure-implementation floor). The Trainium 3 design loss to Alchip (Trainium 2 RDL interposer defects forfeiting the primary socket; Marvell potentially regaining ~500K of 2.5M T3 units on a chiplet path, unconfirmed) is the first material counter-evidence that Marvell can defend even the second seat against geopolitically concentrated implementation specialists. The 2027–2028 test cases are: (a) AWS Trainium 4 socket assignment, (b) Google formalising the April 2026 MPU + inference TPU talks into a signed contract: currently third-seat behind Broadcom's through-2031 lock and MediaTek's fast-follower role.

**Optical DSP duopoly and the LPO self-cannibalisation paradox**. Marvell holds 80%+ share at 800G optical DSP (Inphi-legacy franchise), with Broadcom in secondary share: a duopoly at the PHY layer that has been more durable than the merchant-switching franchise because optical DSP design is bottlenecked by analog-IP teams that no other vendor has scaled. Marvell shipped the industry's first 1.6 Tbps Linear Pluggable Optics (LPO) chipset (200G/lane TIA + laser driver) in 2026: the LPO architecture removes DSP content from short-reach optical modules to save power, compressing ASP and gross margin per port by an estimated 30–40% at equivalent port speed. This is margin-destructive hedging by Marvell against its own DSP monopoly: shipping LPO first secures share in the post-DSP architecture but compresses blended optical gross margin from ~65% (pure DSP) to ~55% (blended) over a 24-month window. Sell-side models that sum DSP growth + LPO growth without re-marking gross-margin assumptions are double-counting; the appropriate framing is that Marvell trades 10pp of structural margin to retain 80%+ unit share through the architectural transition.

**Pricing-power trajectory**. Broadcom's pricing power strengthens across both franchises over 2024–2027. In custom ASIC, switching costs rise with each generation because (i) leading-edge SerDes (224G PAM4 today, 448G entering development) requires shrinking analog-design teams at <=N2 nodes; (ii) HBM4 integration and CoWoS-L packaging create foundry-level orchestration dependencies only Broadcom has at scale; (iii) each TPU/MTIA generation embeds N years of architectural knowledge that a switch to Marvell or Alchip would waste. Jensen Huang's own rebuttal in the April 2026 Dwarkesh interview ("ASIC margin is ~65%, Nvidia is ~70%, what are you really saving?") is an unintended tell: hyperscalers switching from Nvidia GPUs to custom ASICs still pay 65% margins to Broadcom, so Broadcom captures most of the architectural rent that used to accrue to Nvidia. In merchant switching silicon, the Tomahawk 6 / Tomahawk 6-Davisson (CPO) + Jericho 4 (scale-across) + Tomahawk Ultra (scale-up) triple-play provides SKU coverage across every cluster topology; competitors (Marvell, Nvidia, Cisco Silicon One) compete in one dimension at a time. Nvidia's Spectrum-X1600 slipping to H2 2026, six months behind Tomahawk 6, is the single most quantifiable evidence of the widening gap.

**New-entrant threat mapping**. The credible threats are not in scale silicon (where capex + IP depth are prohibitive) but at the edges: (i) connectivity specialists (Astera Labs, Credo) attacking the retimer/AEC/fabric-switch adjacencies with hyperscaler-customer-direct sales; (ii) NVLink Fusion partner silicon (Alchip, MediaTek) enabling hyperscalers to pick Nvidia for scale-up + Broadcom/Marvell for scale-out in the same rack; (iii) hyperscaler in-sourcing of specific IP blocks (Google's own SerDes team hiring, Meta's internal design group), a slow bleed that has not materially compressed Broadcom's revenue share in any year since 2020. The structural observation: every hyperscaler that has attempted full silicon self-sufficiency has ultimately retained Broadcom for the hardest blocks (224G SerDes, advanced packaging, memory interface).

## Macro shifts

**Hyperscaler capex inflation**. 2026 aggregate capex for Amazon ($200B) + Alphabet ($175–185B) + Meta ($115–135B) + Microsoft ($120B+) + Oracle ($50B) = $660–690B, of which ~75% ($450–525B) targets AI infrastructure, a 36% YoY increase on 2025. Hyperscalers raised $108B in debt in 2025 alone; projected debt issuance over the cycle = ~$1.5T. Goldman projects the top AI companies may invest >$500B in 2026. The capex is the direct demand driver for every Broadcom SKU: every dollar of hyperscaler AI capex consumes custom ASIC silicon + switching silicon + DPU/NIC silicon + optical engines + packaging. The macro risk is symmetric: if capex sustains current growth, Broadcom's $100B 2027 AI revenue target is mechanically delivered; if capex plateaus or cuts (AI-monetization gap, rate cycle reversal, hyperscaler ROI scrutiny), multiple compression is immediate because AVGO trades at 35× forward vs 5-year average 22× (60% premium).

**Architectural transition: Ethernet over InfiniBand**. Dell'Oro forecasts Ethernet surpasses InfiniBand in back-end AI networks by 2027. UEC 1.0 closed the performance gap; UEC 1.0.1 (September 2025) added Programmable Congestion Management, Congestion Signaling, and multipath extensions. 800G Ethernet deployment is accelerating 100× faster than prior generation transitions. Broadcom's Tomahawk 6 + Jericho 4 + Tomahawk Ultra triple-play captures the architectural rent across scale-up + scale-out + scale-across tiers. Nvidia's Spectrum-X response is material ($1.46B Q1 2025 revenue, +760% YoY) but the Spectrum-X1600 6-month slip behind Tomahawk 6 signals Nvidia cannot match merchant-silicon cadence in networking.

**Ethernet vs InfiniBand: protocol-level compare**:

| Dimension | InfiniBand (HDR 200G / NDR 400G / XDR 800G) | Ethernet (UEC 800G / 1.6T) |
|---|---|---|
| Loss model | Lossless (credit-based flow control native) | Historically lossy; UEC adds credit-based flow control + link-layer retry |
| RDMA | Native (kernel bypass, zero-copy verbs) | RoCEv2 (RDMA over Converged Ethernet): protocol overlay, now near-parity with UEC |
| Latency (port-to-port) | 90–110 ns | 250–400 ns (Tomahawk 6 scale-out); 250 ns (Tomahawk Ultra scale-up) |
| Routing | Subnet manager: centralised, deterministic | Distributed BGP/EVPN; UEC adds multipath packet spraying |
| Programming model | Verbs API (deeply optimised in CUDA / Magnum IO / GPUDirect) | Sockets + RDMA verbs; UEC standardises AI-specific semantics |
| Scaling ceiling | ~10K endpoints per subnet | ~1M endpoints with UEC + Jericho 4 scale-across |
| Vendor concentration | 100% Nvidia (post-Mellanox 2019) | Multi-vendor: Broadcom, Marvell, Nvidia, Cisco, Arista, system OEMs |
| TCO per port (800G) | $400–600 | $250–400 (merchant-silicon competition) |

**Key products**: InfiniBand → Nvidia Quantum-2 (NDR 400G, 64 ports), Quantum-X800 (XDR 800G, 144 ports, late 2025 volume), ConnectX-7/8 NICs, BlueField-3 DPU. Ethernet AI → Broadcom Tomahawk 6 (102.4 Tbps scale-out), Tomahawk Ultra (51.2 Tbps scale-up), Jericho 4 (51.2 Tbps scale-across), Thor Ultra 800G AI NIC; Nvidia Spectrum-X (Spectrum-4 ASIC + BlueField-3 + ConnectX-8); Marvell Teralynx (12.8 Tbps); Cisco Silicon One. **System vendors**: Arista (Ethernet, Broadcom-silicon), Mellanox/Nvidia (InfiniBand + Spectrum-X), Cisco (Silicon One + NVIDIA partnership), Celestica/Wiwynn (white-box Broadcom).

**Why Ethernet wins by 2027**: (i) UEC 1.0 closed the lossless / RDMA / latency gaps that drove InfiniBand's historical edge; (ii) multi-vendor merchant silicon out-iterates Nvidia's annual cadence (Spectrum-X1600 6-month slip is the empirical proxy); (iii) operator skill base: every hyperscaler operates Ethernet at scale, InfiniBand requires specialised expertise; (iv) 30–40% TCO advantage at 800G holds through XDR transition; (v) AI training clusters past 100K GPUs/XPUs exceed InfiniBand subnet design comfort zone, so Jericho 4 scale-across is the architecturally clean answer. **Why InfiniBand persists in narrow domains**: (i) sub-100 ns latency for HPC simulations (genomics, weather, fusion); (ii) locked-in CUDA + Magnum IO + GPUDirect optimisations; (iii) Nvidia bundles InfiniBand pricing aggressively into GPU sales; (iv) sunk-cost InfiniBand fabrics in existing HPC data centres. Net: InfiniBand survives in classic HPC and Nvidia-bundled new builds; Ethernet (Broadcom-silicon, multi-vendor systems) takes the AI training back-end and all greenfield AI capacity.

**Architectural transition: CPO**. TSMC COUPE in production with TH6-Davisson (200 Gbps/lane) + Broadcom shipping 50K+ CPO switches in 2025 + AMD COUPE risk production Feb 2026 marks the copper-to-optical transition at switch-SoC level. Power reduction (~3× at interconnect layer) becomes mandatory above 100 Tbps. The CPO transition is disproportionately bullish for Broadcom because it locks the switch silicon + optical engine + packaging integration inside one vendor's control plane, widening the moat against system-integrators (Arista, Cisco) who historically assembled switches from components.

**Architectural transition: LPO (DSP self-cannibalisation)**. Linear Pluggable Optics replaces the DSP in short-reach optical modules with linear analog amplification, removing ~50% of optical-module power. Marvell shipped the first 1.6T LPO chipset (200G/lane) ahead of the broader LPO architectural transition, the deliberate strategic choice to cannibalise its own ~65%-margin DSP socket to retain ~80%+ unit share through the architecture change. Sector-level implication: blended optical gross margin compresses from ~65% (pure DSP) toward ~55% (blended DSP + LPO) over 2026–2028, and sell-side models that sum DSP growth + LPO growth without re-marking gross-margin assumptions are double-counting. The non-obvious effect is that LPO weakens Marvell's optical franchise more than Broadcom's because Marvell is the share leader being cannibalised; for hyperscalers, LPO is power-positive (net favourable for capex efficiency); for Nvidia, LPO eliminates a Marvell/Broadcom rent at the cost of intensifying Nvidia's own SerDes-IP exposure on linear interconnect.

**Architectural transition: memory disaggregation / Photonic Fabric**. The 2027–2028 candidate rack primitive: GPU/XPU compute connects to remote HBM pools across a photonic scale-up fabric (16 Tbps/chiplet Gen 1, 64 Tbps/chiplet Gen 2), eliminating the per-chip HBM ceiling that bottlenecks large-context inference and reasoning workloads. Marvell's Celestial AI acquisition ($3.25B, Feb 2026) is the only merchant-silicon bet on this architecture; Nvidia retains its in-house NVLink alternative; Broadcom's CPO + Tomahawk Ultra is adjacent but not a memory-fabric play. The architectural primitive is unproven: if validated by 2027–2028 hyperscaler deployment, it opens a new TAM bucket distinct from CPO and from scale-up Ethernet. If rack architectures stabilise on copper + NVLink + HBM-on-package for three more generations, the Photonic Fabric bet stays sub-$500M revenue and the $3.25B purchase price faces goodwill-impairment risk. The decision-tree is binary at the architecture-validation level rather than incremental.

**Scale-up fabric standards: UALink vs NVLink Fusion vs SUE compare**. Three competing architectures for the intra-rack scale-up socket, the highest-margin networking tier with 3–5× the per-port economics of scale-out. Each is the strategic posture of a different coalition.

| Dimension | UALink 1.0 | NVLink Fusion (NVLink 5.0+) | Broadcom SUE (Tomahawk Ultra) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Origin | Open consortium May 2024: AMD, Intel, Google, Meta, Microsoft, HPE, Broadcom, Cisco | Nvidia proprietary; opened May 2025 to partner silicon (Marvell, MediaTek, Alchip, Astera Labs, Synopsys, Cadence) | Broadcom OCP submission 2026; built on Tomahawk Ultra silicon |
| IP / royalty | Royalty-free open spec | Nvidia retains licensing toll on partner silicon | OCP-open standard; Broadcom monetises silicon, not protocol |
| Bandwidth per accelerator | 800 Gbps target (Spec 1.0) | 1.8 TB/s bidirectional (NVLink 5.0); 3.6 TB/s (NVLink 6.0 roadmap) | 800 Gbps via 224G PAM4; Tomahawk Ultra at 51.2 Tbps |
| Latency (port-to-port) | Target ~250 ns (unproven) | ~150 ns measured (Hopper / Blackwell at NVL72) | 250 ns (Tomahawk Ultra measured) |
| Lane signaling | 200 Gbps/lane on Ethernet PHY (224G PAM4 class) | Custom Nvidia SerDes (224G PAM4 class) | 224G PAM4 Ethernet (Broadcom SerDes) |
| Pod scaling ceiling | 1,024 accelerators per pod | NVL72 today; NVL576 with Vera Rubin H2 2026 | Single-tier fabrics to 100K+ XPUs |
| Switch silicon | Upscale AI dedicated switch: slipped to late 2026; no shipping volume in 2026 | Nvidia NVLink Switch (NVSwitch): shipping in volume since 2024 | Tomahawk Ultra: shipping in volume in 2026 |
| Software / semantic depth | Minimal: protocol-only, no CUDA-equivalent collectives | Deep: CUDA, Magnum IO, GPUDirect, NVLink-Sharp collectives, GPU memory pooling | Standard Ethernet + UEC AI extensions; portable across compute |
| Compute compatibility | AMD MI300/MI400, Intel Gaudi 3+, custom ASICs (UALink-aware) | Nvidia GPUs + partner silicon licensing NVLink Fusion (Marvell custom XPU, MediaTek, Alchip) | Compute-agnostic (any XPU with PCIe/Ethernet attach) |
| Membership coherence | AMD-led; hyperscaler members hedge by also using NVLink Fusion | Nvidia-controlled; partners are silicon implementers, not architectural authority | Broadcom-led OCP, hyperscaler-aligned via OCP |
| Production deployments 2026 | None (waiting on Upscale AI switch) | NVL72 in volume; NVL576 H2 2026 (Vera Rubin) | OpenAI 10 GW build, Anthropic 3.5 GW racks, Meta MTIA reference design |
| Vendor lock-in profile | None: multi-vendor switch silicon eventually | High: Nvidia toll on fabric, Nvidia switch silicon, Nvidia software | Low: Broadcom is silicon vendor but Ethernet is multi-vendor at systems |

**UALink wins on**: openness (no Nvidia toll), royalty-free economics, vendor diversity at switch-silicon layer (eventually), avoidance of Nvidia dependency for non-Nvidia compute. **UALink loses on**: production cadence (Upscale AI switch silicon late 2026 vs Nvidia 2024 production, a 2-year gap during the 2026–2027 capex peak), absence of CUDA-equivalent collective software, latency at fabric maturity unproven, single startup-vendor switch supply, coalition cohesion (Google, Meta, Microsoft are also NVLink Fusion partners, hedging against AMD's UALink pure-play).

**NVLink Fusion wins on**: production maturity (shipping at scale since 2024 Hopper era), measured latency (~150 ns at NVL72 scale), software integration depth (CUDA/Magnum IO/GPUDirect/NVLink-Sharp), bandwidth leadership (1.8 TB/s NVLink 5.0; 3.6 TB/s roadmap), Nvidia financial backing, partner-silicon ecosystem (Marvell $2B March 2026 deal as proof point). **NVLink Fusion loses on**: lock-in economics (Nvidia retains toll on partner silicon, exactly what UALink members wanted to avoid), strategic dependency for non-Nvidia compute (AMD, Intel, sovereign-cloud customers cannot use it for ideological reasons), partner authority asymmetry (silicon partners are implementers, not architectural decision-makers), Nvidia controls fabric-layer margin capture.

**Broadcom SUE / Tomahawk Ultra wins on**: production maturity (shipping in volume in 2026, only merchant scale-up silicon at scale), open standard (OCP-submitted), compute-agnostic (works with any XPU: Google TPU, Meta MTIA, OpenAI XPU, Anthropic, AWS Trainium, AMD/Intel GPUs), no vendor toll on protocol, hyperscaler-validated deployments (OpenAI 10 GW, Anthropic 3.5 GW). **SUE loses on**: latency parity (250 ns vs NVLink 150 ns, material for tightly-coupled inference workloads), absence of CUDA-equivalent collective software, dependence on UEC AI extensions still maturing, no integrated GPU-memory-pool semantics like NVLink-Sharp.

**Strategic conclusion**:
- **UALink** is the open-coalition response to NVLink dominance, politically attractive but operationally fragile. It needs Upscale AI to ship competitive switch silicon, AMD/Intel to deliver compute that justifies an alternate fabric, and the consortium to align on roadmap cadence. Coalition cohesion is the principal risk: Google/Meta/Microsoft are paying NVLink Fusion partners simultaneously, so UALink is effectively an AMD-led pure-play with hedging contributors.
- **NVLink Fusion** is Nvidia's containment strategy: rather than fight a multi-vendor open standard from outside, Nvidia opens its fabric to partners while retaining the architectural authority and the toll. Marvell's $2B March 2026 deal is the tell: even hyperscaler design partners trade independence for Nvidia integration when the alternative (UALink) is not yet shipping.
- **Broadcom SUE / Tomahawk Ultra** is the third path that wins in the standards-war ambiguity window. It is the only merchant scale-up silicon shipping in volume in 2026, deployed at OpenAI and Anthropic, and serves as the substrate for any scale-up topology a hyperscaler chooses without forcing a UALink-vs-NVLink-Fusion commitment. The 2-year cadence gap (2026–2028) before UALink switch silicon matures is the window where Broadcom captures architectural rent, and the installed base built in that window creates path dependency past 2028.

**Investment translation**: AVGO benefits from any outcome: it captures Tomahawk Ultra revenue regardless of which standard "wins" because greenfield 2026–2027 deployments are pre-commitment and SUE is the available answer. MRVL is binary on NVLink Fusion winning: its $2B-backed silicon-partner role strands if UALink takes share by 2028. NVDA wins fabric-economics if NVLink Fusion entrenches but loses partner trust (every partner is by definition a non-Nvidia compute customer). AMD/Intel are leveraged on UALink succeeding but face compound execution risk (Upscale AI switch + their own compute roadmaps + consortium alignment). Per the existing §Investor heuristics → "scale-up is the real 2026 battle" non-consensus insight: AVGO scale-up payoff is robust to standard selection; MRVL scale-up payoff is binary on selection.

**Procurement normalisation: second-source structural slot**. No major hyperscaler accepts single-vendor lock-in on multi-billion-dollar custom-silicon programs. The procurement consequence: every Broadcom RFP is shopped to a credible alternate (Marvell, Alchip, MediaTek, GUC). The macro effect is that Marvell's revenue floor is structurally durable even when its technical position lags, but the same procurement logic caps its pricing power at the ~5pp gross-margin discount to Broadcom (MRVL ~60% non-GAAP vs AVGO ~65%). The 2027–2028 fragmentation vector is that hyperscalers add a third design partner (Google now using Broadcom + Marvell + MediaTek across different chip classes), splitting the second-source slot and compressing ASPs further. The empirical question: does second-source procurement evolve into three-source procurement, and at what point does the resulting ASP compression reach merchant-foundry economics? The compression first becomes visible in ASIC gross margins moving below ~60%, and is the leading bear-case indicator for both AVGO and MRVL.

**Geopolitical concentration: TSMC**. 92% of leading-edge foundry output (<=N3), 100% of CoWoS, ~95% of advanced packaging sit inside 100-mile PLA strike window per the April 2026 TSM stress test ([[Research/2026-04-19 - TSM - Stress Test]]). Every Broadcom XPU (Google TPU, Meta MTIA, OpenAI XPU, Anthropic racks) runs on TSMC N3/N2 Kaohsiung. Every Tomahawk / Jericho / Tomahawk Ultra SoC runs on TSMC N3P. A Taiwan blockade or conflict would force a 2–4 year customer-transfer window to Samsung Foundry or Intel 18A, during which the entire sector's revenue collapses to Arizona/Japan/Germany fab output (~5–8% of current TSMC leading-edge capacity through 2028). The risk is a sector-level tail rather than Broadcom-specific, and the current 35× AVGO forward multiple does not discount it.

**Hyperscaler in-sourcing vector: ASIC**. Google has been designing TPUs for 13 years and still partners with Broadcom for SerDes + packaging + TSMC orchestration. Meta entered MTIA in 2020 and has committed to four more generations with Broadcom through 2027+. Amazon's Trainium replaced Marvell with Alchip on Trainium 3, a design-partner change, not a full in-source. The structural conclusion: hyperscalers are consolidating ASIC architecture ownership (JAX, XLA, MTIA software, Inferentia Neuron SDK) but not ASIC implementation ownership. The IP depth required for <=N2 leading-edge silicon + HBM4 integration + advanced packaging remains concentrated in Broadcom/Marvell/Alchip. The binary in-sourcing scenario the market persistently prices is not empirically consistent with any hyperscaler's actual revealed behavior through April 2026.

**Hyperscaler in-sourcing vector: switching silicon**. The switching-silicon in-sourcing risk is structurally lower than the ASIC in-sourcing risk and is not materialising in the data through April 2026. **Current programmes**: no major hyperscaler operates a production in-house merchant-class switching SoC. Past attempts: Google published the Aquila research switch (SIGCOMM 2022) but never productionised it for general datacenter switching; Meta evaluated alternatives but runs zero in-house switch-ASIC programmes through 2026; AWS uses Broadcom Tomahawk for general DC switching plus AWS-designed Nitro NICs and Trainium NeuronLink for specific in-rack interconnect, with no general-purpose merchant switch-silicon attempt; Microsoft has no in-house switch-silicon programme; Alibaba/Tencent use Broadcom Tomahawk plus selected Marvell Teralynx. **Switching-silicon share inside hyperscale data centres (April 2026 estimate, blending Linley / 650 Group / Counterpoint / management commentary)**: Broadcom 80–90% (Tomahawk 4/5/6/Ultra + Jericho 3/4 across all six US hyperscalers + ByteDance); Nvidia Spectrum-X ~5–10% rising fastest (concentrated at Microsoft Azure for Nvidia-GPU clusters and Oracle Cloud); Marvell Teralynx ~3–5% (selected mid-radix and edge-DC sockets, not back-end AI training); Cisco Silicon One ~1–3% (mostly Microsoft + selected enterprise); Intel post-Tofino ~0%; ODM/white-box vendors (Celestica, Wiwynn, Quanta, Edgecore) are the channel through which Broadcom silicon reaches hyperscalers, not a separate silicon source. **Why hyperscalers don't in-source switching silicon at the same pace as ASIC**: (i) merchant switching silicon is already 80–90% concentrated with no architectural differentiation gap to close: every cluster needs the same switching primitives (no analog to the JAX/XLA/MTIA-software architectural rent that justifies hyperscaler ASIC investment); (ii) switching silicon does not bottleneck AI training the way compute architecture does: owning the switch SoC saves cost per port but does not unlock workload performance; (iii) Tomahawk cadence (51.2 Tbps in 2023, 102.4 Tbps in March 2026, 204.8 Tbps roadmap by 2028) outpaces any plausible in-house programme that requires 3–5 years per generation; (iv) the software stack (SONiC, SAI, P4) is already open and standardised: no proprietary IP advantage to capture by owning silicon; (v) 224G PAM4 / 448G SerDes IP depth is the binding constraint, the same scarce-analog-design-team problem that caps ASIC in-sourcing. **Where in-sourcing is happening at the IP-block level**: Google designs its own SerDes for ICI (intra-pod TPU interconnect) but pairs with Broadcom for the inter-pod Apollo OCS substrate and for TPU silicon implementation; Meta licenses selected IP from Open Compute but designs no switch SoC; AWS Nitro and NeuronLink are NIC and intra-rack interconnect silicon, not general datacenter switching. **Verdict**: Broadcom's 80–90% merchant switching share is at structural risk from merchant competitors (Nvidia Spectrum-X, Marvell Teralynx, Cisco Silicon One) rather than from hyperscaler in-sourcing. The empirical absence of any general-switching ASIC programme at any hyperscaler in 2026, despite a decade of ASIC architectural-ownership consolidation on the compute side, is the strongest indicator that the merchant-switching franchise is structurally more durable than the merchant-ASIC franchise. The bear case for switching silicon is competitive-share erosion (Nvidia Spectrum-X gaining at NVL72 sockets, Marvell winning second-source at edge-DC sockets), not hyperscaler vertical integration.

**Apple in-sourcing vector**. Apple Proxima chip in-sources Wi-Fi/BT from Broadcom, replacing ~$2.7B of FY2026 revenue. RF FBAR filter business (~$2.7B, 65% of Apple-related revenue) is physics-gated and harder to replicate. Apple's long-term intent to in-source more of its RF stack is the slow-bleed risk the market correctly prices as a steady-state headwind rather than a binary cliff.

**China geopolitical exposure**. FY2024 China revenue ~$10.5B (~20% of total, down from 30% historical). Trade-sanction tail is real but not sector-unique; Huawei Ascend's vertical integration caps the recoverable China TAM regardless of US policy. The more material read-through: every major non-China hyperscaler plus ByteDance (which uses both Huawei Ascend and Broadcom-designed chips) concentrates AI compute spend in a TSMC-dependent supply chain.

**Value-chain shift: software layer**. VMware / CA / Symantec contribute ~35% of Broadcom revenue as high-margin recurring software annuity. In a hypothetical AI-capex slowdown, the software segment decouples Broadcom from pure semiconductor cyclicality: this is the structural advantage over pure-play peers (Marvell, Nvidia) and the reason Broadcom's effective beta to AI capex is lower than its semiconductor revenue mix suggests. 30K VMware customer migrations to Nutanix + EU CISPE complaints + AT&T/Siemens lawsuits validate Tan's "shrink-the-base, raise-ARPU" playbook only if net revenue on Global 2000 accounts grows faster than churn; the bear-case metric to monitor is VMware net revenue retention, which management has not yet disclosed at granular cohort level.

## Investor heuristics

**Consensus frame: sector**. The sell-side consensus frames the sector as a binary substitution: "AI ASIC + Ethernet play vs Nvidia GPU + InfiniBand play", the "Android to Nvidia's Apple" narrative for Broadcom, and the "Open Ecosystem Champion vs Broadcom Vertical Integration" narrative for Marvell. Both frames are partially correct but structurally understated. The empirical reality is that every major AI cluster contains Nvidia compute + Broadcom networking silicon + Marvell optical DSP + Marvell or Alchip second-source ASIC content concurrently: substitution dynamics operate within franchises (Tomahawk vs Spectrum-X within switching; Marvell vs Alchip within design services) rather than between tickers. Revenue growth for AVGO does not require Nvidia to lose share, and revenue growth for MRVL does not require AVGO to lose share. The pair is more accurately framed as "primary supplier (AVGO) + structurally locked second source (MRVL) + niche specialists (Alchip, MediaTek, Astera Labs)" rather than as competitors fighting for the same wallet.

**What is priced in: AVGO**. 35× forward PE (vs 5-year average 22×, sector average ~27×) embeds (i) $100B+ AI semiconductor revenue by 2027 per Hock Tan's guidance, (ii) sustained 60–70% custom ASIC share through 2027, (iii) 80–90% merchant switching silicon share defended, (iv) VMware net revenue growth despite 30K customer churn, (v) hyperscaler capex continuation at $600B+ annually through 2027, (vi) no Taiwan tail event, (vii) Apple in-sourcing as gradual rather than step-function. The multiple is defensible if each holds; compression is rapid if any two fail simultaneously. The trailing PE of 62× is GAAP noise from VMware acquisition accounting and should be disregarded.

**What is priced in: MRVL**. 36× forward PE FY27E / 26× FY28E (vs 5-year average 23×, sector ~27×) and +168% trailing twelve months to ~$158 embeds (i) $14–16B FY28 revenue (from $8.2B FY26, +30% FY27 guide), (ii) custom-silicon FY28 doubling to ~$3B from $1.5B FY26, (iii) Celestial Photonic Fabric ramp to $500M Q4 FY28 / $1B by end-FY29 on the acquisition roadmap, (iv) Google MPU + inference TPU exploratory talks converting to formal contract in FY27, (v) AWS Trainium 4 design-partner socket retention after the T3 primary loss, (vi) NVLink Fusion winning the 2027–2028 hyperscaler scale-up rack standard against UALink, (vii) blended optical gross margin holding above ~58% as LPO compresses DSP. The multiple cushion is thinner than AVGO's because four of the seven embedded assumptions are execution-dependent on a management team that just mis-executed Trainium 3 advanced packaging.

**Where consensus could be wrong: AVGO bull direction**. (1) The $100B 2027 AI revenue target may be materially understated. Mizuho estimates Google + Anthropic deals alone generate $21B AI revenue in 2026 and $42B in 2027, plus Meta 1GW + OpenAI 10GW + ByteDance. The $73B backlog disclosed Q1 FY2026 is an 18-month visibility window that traditional semiconductor companies have never had. (2) Scale-across (Jericho 4, HyperPort) is a TAM expansion not in consensus models: the fourth networking tier monetizes the geographic distribution of training workloads that did not exist as a workload pattern three years ago. (3) CPO switch economics (>3× power reduction at 100 Tbps) create silent adoption lock-in: every hyperscaler that deploys TH6-Davisson at scale incurs architectural path dependency. (4) VMware cohort-level ARPU math may net positive even with 30K churn if Global 2000 renewal pricing holds. (5) The Nvidia Spectrum-X1600 6-month slip is a proxy for a widening networking-cadence gap, not a one-time execution miss.

**Where consensus could be wrong: AVGO bear direction**. (1) The "frenemy" dynamic with hyperscalers reaches inflection around 2027–2028 if Meta or Google add a second ASIC design partner beyond Broadcom (already happening at Google with MediaTek for inference chips). Design-partner fragmentation compresses ASP even without share loss. (2) AI-monetization gap (the J.P. Morgan $650B annual revenue threshold vs current ~$200B AI revenue in production) is an asymmetric risk: capex decelerates on the downside faster than consensus models accommodate. (3) TSMC concentration tail is materially underpriced in AVGO-specific risk premium; sector-level, a 2027 Xi Taiwan action collapses 85–95% of enterprise value in a multi-quarter window per [[Research/2026-04-19 - TSM - Stress Test]]. (4) Nvidia's NVLink Fusion + $2B Marvell deal is an ecosystem response that could slow Ethernet's scale-up share gain; UEC vs NVLink Fusion + UALink remains contested through 2028. (5) Hock Tan succession is a latent risk; Charlie Kawwas is the internal heir apparent but has not operated the full capital-allocation / M&A function that defines the Broadcom playbook.

**Where consensus could be wrong: MRVL bull direction**. (1) Photonic Fabric is a memory-disaggregation primitive, not a CPO re-skin: if the 2027–2028 rack architecture shifts to remote HBM pools across photonic scale-up fabrics, Celestial is the only merchant option outside Nvidia NVLink and the $500M FY28 run-rate guide understates by orders of magnitude. (2) Second-source procurement is a structural feature not a transitional state: every multi-billion-dollar hyperscaler ASIC RFP is bid by Marvell regardless of technical gap, durably anchoring revenue floor. (3) Optical DSP duopoly is more durable than consensus credits because LPO does not address long-reach scale-out where 1.6T/3.2T DSP economics persist; the LPO threat is short-reach-only and Marvell retains the analog silicon socket. (4) NVLink Fusion as legitimisation: Nvidia investing $2B March 2026 implicitly accepts that hyperscalers mix non-Nvidia compute with Nvidia scale-up, so Marvell is structurally inside the ecosystem rather than competing against it. (5) AWS Trainium 4 design-partner socket reset: the T3 loss was packaging-execution-driven (RDL interposer), not commercial-relationship-driven, and the Marvell-AWS roadmap has more T4/T5 surface area than the loss implies.

**Where consensus could be wrong: MRVL bear direction**. (1) Trainium 3 is a management-competence red flag rather than a one-off. A design-services firm that fails the advanced-packaging hand-off has demonstrated it cannot ship the category-defining capability; the FY28 doubling guide is structurally overstated unless T4 socket allocation, Google contract formalisation, and Meta/Microsoft re-engagement scope all firm up by Q3 FY27. (2) Nvidia's $2B is a UALink containment move dressed as partnership: Nvidia historically invests in suppliers it wants captive. NVLink Fusion pulls Marvell's custom-silicon customers into a Nvidia-defined fabric at the moment UALink would otherwise have pulled them out. The "open ecosystem champion" positioning becomes conditional on NVLink Fusion not swallowing it. (3) LPO compresses DSP ASP by 30–40% per port at equivalent speed; sell-side models that sum DSP growth + LPO growth without re-marking gross-margin assumptions are double-counting. Blended optical gross margin compresses from ~65% to ~55% over 24 months, a 10pp structural margin compression that derates the multiple more than the growth story supports. (4) Google engagement is third-seat behind Broadcom's through-2031 lock and MediaTek's fast-follower role; Marvell's Google contribution to the FY28 doubling is materially smaller than the headline implies and may be roadmap participation rather than revenue. (5) The +168% TTM rally has priced the bull path; forward P/E 36× leaves no cushion for any execution slip on Celestial integration, Trainium 4 socket, or LPO blended margin.

**Non-consensus insight: chokepoint arithmetic**. Merchant switching silicon share (80–90%) is structurally more durable than custom ASIC share (60–70%) because switching is compute-agnostic: every cluster, regardless of compute vendor, consumes Tomahawk/Jericho. Custom ASIC franchise is customer-specific: loss of Google or Meta would be material. Sell-side modeling typically weights custom ASIC as the high-growth vector and networking as the stable franchise; the inverse relationship of durability to volatility matters for risk-adjusted TAM modeling. The Jensen Huang Dwarkesh admission ("ASIC margins ~65% vs Nvidia ~70%") reframes the hyperscaler shift from GPUs to ASICs as a ~5-point margin transfer to customers, not the market-implied assumption that ASICs cannibalize Broadcom. The same arithmetic compounds at MRVL ~60% non-GAAP: every "second seat" win is structurally a lower-margin seat than the incumbent's, capping how high MRVL can ever credibly close the AVGO 65% vs MRVL 60% gap.

**Non-consensus insight: scale-up is the real 2026 battle**. Consensus fixates on scale-out (Tomahawk 6 vs Spectrum-X1600) because it is the visible topology tier. The contested socket is scale-up: Nvidia NVLink + Fusion vs Broadcom SUE (OCP) vs AMD/Intel/Meta/Microsoft UALink. Scale-up unit economics per port are 3–5× scale-out because intra-rack radix + latency tolerance are tighter. Whoever wins scale-up architecture wins the compute-adjacent silicon margin pool, and the fact that UALink dedicated switch silicon slipped to late 2026 while Broadcom's Tomahawk Ultra is already shipping as the SUE substrate is an empirically dominant position that sell-side has not fully modeled. The MRVL angle: NVLink Fusion is the third path; if it wins, MRVL is the non-Nvidia silicon beneficiary inside Nvidia's ecosystem; if UALink wins, MRVL's $2B-backed fabric bet strands. The Marvell scale-up payoff is binary on standard selection; the Broadcom scale-up payoff is robust to which standard wins because Tomahawk Ultra/SUE is the third-path substrate either way.

**Non-consensus insight: the "software insurance" is undervalued (AVGO-specific)**. VMware + CA + Symantec generate ~35% of revenue at software-franchise margins and are structurally decorrelated from AI capex. In a hypothetical AI-capex bust scenario, Broadcom's trailing revenue drawdown would be ~20–30% (semiconductor-segment decline + software base stable), vs Nvidia's ~60–70% (all-semiconductor drawdown). The effective revenue beta to AI capex is meaningfully lower than market-cap beta reflects; pure-AI investors underweight AVGO relative to NVDA precisely because software drag is mistaken for diversification dilution rather than tail-risk hedging. MRVL has no equivalent decorrelation: 100% of revenue is semiconductor, 75% is data-center, the AI-capex beta is full. In a sector-cycle derate (forward P/E compressing from 36× to 22–24× sector trough), MRVL has 40–50% multiple compression risk before any thesis damage; AVGO at 35× has 30–35% compression risk for the same cycle event because the software base stabilises the EPS denominator.

**Non-consensus insight: second-seat ceiling is a permanent feature**. The procurement logic that hands Marvell its second-source slot (hyperscalers refuse single-vendor lock-in) also caps Marvell's pricing power. The empirical evidence is the structural ~5pp non-GAAP gross-margin gap (MRVL ~60% vs AVGO ~65%) that has held across the 2018–2026 acquisition period despite four consolidations. The next-decade pattern: as hyperscaler design-partner fragmentation expands (Google adding MediaTek as a third partner; Meta likely adding a second to Broadcom; AWS already running Marvell + Alchip in parallel), the second-seat ceiling tightens further toward Alchip's ~30% pure-services floor. The investment implication: MRVL multiple compression is an asymmetric risk vs AVGO because the structural margin gap is a function of customer procurement strategy, not a function of Marvell's product investment.

**Paired trade: MRVL as AVGO proxy and the multiple-vs-growth math**. MRVL revenue direction co-moves with AVGO (both rise/fall with hyperscaler AI capex), but the magnitude, quality, and risk profile diverge materially.

**Growth comparison FY26–FY28**

| Metric | AVGO | MRVL |
|---|---|---|
| FY26 total revenue | ~$60B (semis $30B + software $21.5B + organic) | $8.2B |
| AI-segment FY26 → FY27 | $22B → $45B (Goldman), +105% | Custom-silicon $1.5B → ~$2.2B (+45%) |
| Total revenue growth FY27 | ~+20% (software base dilutes) | +30% (guide) |
| FY28 total trajectory | $100B+ AI franchise per Hock Tan | $14–16B total |
| Beta to AI capex | Partial (semis ~65%, software ~35%) | Full (data-center ~75%, semis 100%) |

**Multiple comparison (April 2026)**

| Metric | AVGO | MRVL |
|---|---|---|
| Forward P/E (FY27E) | 35× | 36× |
| Forward P/E (FY28E) | ~28× implied | 26× |
| 5-year average P/E | 22× | 23× |
| Sector average P/E | 27× | 27× |
| Premium to history | 60% (FY27) / 27% (FY28) | 60% (FY27) / 13% (FY28) |
| PEG total (FY27 fwd) | ~1.75 | ~1.20 |
| PEG AI-segment | 0.50–0.70 (FY27 fwd) | 0.65–0.87 (FY28 implied) |
| Non-GAAP gross margin | ~75% blended (semis ~65%, software ~88%) | ~60% blended (DSP ~65%, ASIC ~55%) |

**Is the 5pp gross-margin gap minimal for a second-source laggard?** Empirically yes (5pp is small), but the gap is the equilibrium settled by a four-year procurement-pattern test (post-Inphi 2021 through Q1 FY26). Every hyperscaler RFP that creates the second-source slot also enforces the discount. MRVL has not closed this gap despite four major IP acquisitions (Inphi, Innovium, Aquantia, Celestial). The right framing is that "5pp is durable" rather than "5pp is small": it is a structural procurement discount, not a product-investment-fixable gap. As hyperscaler design-partner fragmentation expands (Google adding MediaTek as a third partner; Meta likely adding a second), the second-seat ceiling tightens further toward Alchip's ~30% pure-services floor.

**If MRVL matches AVGO growth, does it trade at a cheaper multiple?** On forward FY28 earnings, MRVL at 26× already trades at a 25% multiple discount to AVGO at ~28× implied, but the discount reflects (i) absence of the VMware/CA/Symantec software annuity that decouples AVGO from pure semiconductor cyclicality, (ii) the Trainium 3 execution miss that flagged management-competence risk, (iii) thinner cushion in the seven embedded MRVL assumptions vs AVGO's seven (Photonic Fabric ramp, Google MPU contract conversion, Trainium 4 socket retention, NVLink Fusion winning scale-up: four of the seven are execution-dependent on a team that just mis-executed). PEG-adjusted, MRVL FY28 PEG ~0.65–0.87 is cheaper than AVGO total PEG ~1.75 but comparable to AVGO AI-segment PEG ~0.50–0.70, so the apparent multiple discount disappears when adjusted for AVGO's recurring-software stabilizer.

**Pair-trade conclusion**: MRVL is a Broadcom proxy in revenue direction (both correlate to AI capex) but not in revenue magnitude or quality. MRVL is more leveraged: full beta to AI capex (no software hedge) and execution risk concentrated in 4 of 7 embedded assumptions. The 5pp gross margin gap is durable. Sector-cycle derate exposure: in a forward P/E compress from 36× to 22–24× sector trough, MRVL has 40–50% multiple compression risk before any thesis damage; AVGO at 35× has 30–35% compression risk for the same cycle event because the software base stabilises the EPS denominator. The implication: long AVGO / short MRVL is a way to express "sector AI capex slows but does not crash" (MRVL underperforms because growth converges to AVGO without the multiple cushion to absorb derate); long MRVL / short AVGO is a way to express "AI capex re-accelerates and Photonic Fabric validates by 2028" (MRVL outperforms because growth-multiple expansion compounds against AVGO's already-rich multiple). Default direction: long AVGO / short MRVL is the cheaper expression of the cycle-derate risk that is the dominant 2026–2027 macro tail.

**Non-consensus insight: Photonic Fabric is the asymmetric MRVL upside**. The $3.25B Celestial purchase price prices the Photonic Fabric acquisition as a lottery ticket; the $500M Q4 FY28 run-rate guide prices it as already-validated. Both framings can be wrong in opposite directions. If memory-disaggregation becomes the 2027–2028 rack primitive (the architectural primitive change required to break the per-chip HBM ceiling for trillion-parameter MoE inference and reasoning workloads), Photonic Fabric is the only merchant scale-up optical option outside Nvidia NVLink, and $500M understates by orders of magnitude. If rack architectures stabilise on copper + NVLink + HBM-on-package for three more generations, $500M is the ceiling not the floor and the $3.25B faces goodwill impairment. The asymmetry favours MRVL on a sufficiently long horizon (5+ years) regardless of the standard-vs-photonic-fabric race in 2027–2028 because photonic interconnect is on the architectural roadmap of every hyperscaler, but the 24-month execution timeline depends on the same advanced-packaging team that mis-executed Trainium 3.

**Value-layer read + July 2026 multiple inversion** (per [[Research/2026-07-10 - MRVL vs AVGO - Competitive Comparison]]). The Value Layer Monopoly lens sharpens the pair-trade: AVGO owns the layers everything above must traverse (80–90% merchant switching + the 224G-SerDes/CoWoS-L/HBM4 ASIC-IP layer + the VMware software annuity), infrastructure-layer, moat-widening; MRVL is a layer-renter at the ASIC seat (rents hyperscaler sockets, sits inside the Nvidia NVLink perimeter) that owns exactly one durable layer (80%+ 800G DSP) and is running a binary bet on owning a new one (Celestial memory-fabric, a layer AVGO does not contest). That asymmetry, owned layers vs rented seat, is the durable source of the ~15pp blended-GM and ~5pp ASIC-GM gaps, not a product-investment-fixable deficit. The April paired-trade multiple framing above has since inverted: MRVL's business ran ahead of its own bull case (FY28 guide raised to $16.5B, custom silicon >$10B FY29, Q1 FY27 +28%), and after the July re-rate MRVL trades ~54× forward vs AVGO ~23× (post the Jun-3 chips-only-pivot derate that made AVGO the cheapest AI-complex name); MRVL now carries a ~2.3× multiple premium, reversing the "MRVL is the cheaper multiple" leg of the April pair-trade. Read: the AVGO-vs-MRVL gap is now a quality/margin gap, not a growth gap; the May [[Research/2026-05-24 - Semiconductor Portfolio Rebalancing - synthesis]] EXIT-MRVL call is stale on the numbers but its relative quality ranking (AVGO higher) survives the layer analysis.
